paper_metadata.title: Quantum unary approach to option pricing

summary: The paper proposes a unary‑encoded gate‑based quantum algorithm for European option pricing using amplitude estimation. Simulations with 8 unary qubits (8 bins) under a Black–Scholes model show improved noise robustness relative to a binary encoding and estimate a reference payoff of 0.1595, while maintaining <1% discretization error with ~100 bins; the claimed advantage is the standard quadratic sampling speedup of amplitude estimation over classical Monte Carlo.

experiments.description: Unary gate-based quantum algorithm for European option pricing under the Black-Scholes model, evaluated via classical simulation in ideal and noisy settings, including amplitude distribution loading, payoff estimation, and iterative amplitude estimation with post-selection.

algorithm.variant: Unary option-pricing algorithm with iterative amplitude estimation and post-selection
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Initial unary state prepared by applying a single X gate to the middle qubit; amplitude-distributor angles computed classically from the target probability distribution

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Unary basis: one qubit in |1> identifies each asset-price bin; 8 bins used in simulations with 8 unary qubits
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate the expected payoff of a European call option, E[max(S_T-K,0)], under the Black-Scholes log-normal distribution
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Post-selection on measurements that remain in the unary subspace; ancilla outcome |1> encodes payoff probability
problem_formulation.num_ancilla_qubits: >=1 (one payoff ancilla; AE may require additional ancillas depending on AE variant)

problem_instance.description: Single European call option pricing under Black-Scholes with a discretized log-normal asset-price distribution

dataset_specification.description: Synthetic Black-Scholes distribution; price range up to three standard deviations from the mean

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Classical computation of the target log-normal distribution and binning into unary basis states; exact classical payoff used as reference from high-resolution discretization (10^4 bins)
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Classical simulations in Qiskit; 100 experiments with 10^4 samples each for distribution-loading and noisy-payoff studies; AE experiments repeated 100 times; some larger-bin AE studies repeated 10 times

noise_model.noise_type: depolarizing noise on single- and two-qubit gates plus symmetric measurement error

implementation_details.classical_solver: classical Monte Carlo / classical high-resolution discretization for reference values
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Compute Black-Scholes log-normal distribution and derive gate angles for amplitude distributor; determine strike-dependent controlled rotations
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Estimate payoff from ancilla probability and multiply by normalization factor; discard non-unary measurement outcomes via post-selection

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: AE precision improves with more iterations; noisy performance degrades for larger M

speedup_claims.conditions: Amplitude Estimation with idealized assumptions; quadratic reduction in number of circuit runs / samples needed for a target precision
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper notes this is only achievable when the probability distribution can be loaded efficiently; NISQ noise and post-selection reduce practical advantage.

speedup_claims.factor: better than binary for fewer than about 100 bins
speedup_claims.conditions: Practical NISQ-like settings with limited qubits and noise; based on gate-count comparison and simulations
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a practical crossover claim, not an asymptotic one; binary has better asymptotic qubit scaling but worse gate overhead and connectivity requirements.

speedup_claims.factor: O(n) gates for unary amplitude distribution and O(kappa n) controlled-Ry gates
speedup_claims.caveats: Unary uses linearly many qubits, while binary uses logarithmically many qubits.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(n) gates for amplitude distribution and O(κn) controlled-Ry gates for payoff; iterative AE used for estimation
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Monte Carlo sampling with O(1/ε^2) samples for precision ε
complexity_analysis.crossover_n: around fewer than 100 bins/qubits for practical gate-count advantage per paper discussion

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: authors argue unary circuits may be preferable for <~100 bins due to gate overhead and noise, but no demonstrated runtime crossover vs classical Monte Carlo
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Fault‑tolerant implementation of amplitude estimation with efficient state preparation for the log‑normal distribution and many more logical qubits than the 8‑qubit simulations; scalable amplitude loading and low‑error circuits required
limiting_factors: Probability distribution loading requires classical preprocessing and parameter calculation
Unary encoding requires O(n) qubits rather than O(log n)
Amplitude estimation advantage requires many coherent circuit repetitions
Simulations only performed on very small systems (8 bins)
Noise strongly limits AE iterations on NISQ devices

notes: hardware.type inferred as simulator_noisy because the paper states simulations were carried out in Qiskit with depolarizing and measurement noise, and no real QPU is named.

circuit_depth not explicitly given as a single total value for the full simulated experiment; only module-level scaling and asymptotic depths are reported, so it is left inferred/null where not directly stated.
num_qubits=8 comes from the simulation setup for the unary algorithm (8 unary qubits corresponding to 8 bins).
The paper claims a theoretical quadratic speedup via amplitude estimation but does not experimentally demonstrate quantum advantage.
All results are classical simulations (ideal and noisy) with small toy instances (8 bins).
Comparison with classical Monte Carlo is theoretical rather than runtime benchmarking.
